difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY because it tests one concept (covariance of two indicator variables) on a four-outcome sample space, where E[X], E[Y] and E[XY] are each read off directly, in about a minute.
stem:
Two fair coins are tossed independently. $X$ is a random variable that takes a value of 1 if both tosses are heads and 0 otherwise. $Y$ is a random variable that takes a value of 1 if at least one of the tosses is heads and 0 otherwise.

The value of the covariance of $X$ and $Y$ is ______ (rounded off to **three** decimal places).

solution.quick: $X$ indicates HH and $Y$ indicates at least one H, so $E[X] = \tfrac14$ and $E[Y] = \tfrac34$. Since $X = 1$ forces $Y = 1$, $XY = X$ and $E[XY] = \tfrac14$. Then $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = \tfrac14 - \tfrac14 \cdot \tfrac34 = \tfrac1{16} = 0.0625$, which is **0.063** to three decimal places (the key accepts 0.062 to 0.063).

steps.title: Sample space and the values of X, Y and XY
steps.body:
The two fair coins give four equally likely outcomes, each with probability $\tfrac14$:

| Outcome | Probability | $X$ | $Y$ | $XY$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HH | $1/4$ | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| HT | $1/4$ | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| TH | $1/4$ | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| TT | $1/4$ | 0 | 0 | 0 |

steps.title: Means of X and Y
steps.body:
Each variable is an indicator, so its mean is the probability of its event:

$$E[X] = P(\text{HH}) = \tfrac14, \qquad E[Y] = P(\text{HH, HT or TH}) = \tfrac34.$$

steps.title: Mean of the product XY
steps.body:
$XY = 1$ only when both $X = 1$ and $Y = 1$, which happens only on HH. (In fact $X = 1$ implies $Y = 1$, so $XY = X$.) Therefore

$$E[XY] = P(\text{HH}) = \tfrac14.$$

steps.title: Round to three decimal places
steps.body: The exact value $0.0625$ lies exactly halfway between $0.062$ and $0.063$. The usual round-half-up rule gives $0.063$. The official key range, $0.062$ to $0.063$, covers both neighbouring three-decimal values.

solution.finalAnswer: **0.0625**, which is **0.063** to three decimal places (the official key accepts 0.062 to 0.063)
solution.teaching:
**Covariance.** For random variables $X$ and $Y$,

$$\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = E\big[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])\big] = E[XY] - E[X]\,E[Y].$$

It is positive when $X$ and $Y$ tend to be above their means together, and negative when one tends to be high while the other is low. Independent variables have zero covariance, although zero covariance does not imply independence.

**Indicator (Bernoulli) variables.** An indicator $\mathbb{1}_A$ equals 1 if event $A$ happens and 0 otherwise. Two facts make indicators easy to work with:

- $E[\mathbb{1}_A] = P(A)$: the mean of a Bernoulli variable is its success probability.
- $\mathbb{1}_A\,\mathbb{1}_B = \mathbb{1}_{A \cap B}$: the product is 1 only when both events happen.

Hence, for indicators,

$$\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbb{1}_A, \mathbb{1}_B) = P(A \cap B) - P(A)\,P(B).$$

This is zero exactly when $A$ and $B$ are independent events, and positive when knowing that $A$ happened makes $B$ more likely.

**Nested events.** If $A \subseteq B$, then $A \cap B = A$ and the formula becomes $P(A) - P(A)P(B) = P(A)\,(1 - P(B)) = P(A)\,P(B^c)$.

**Back to this question.** $X$ indicates $A = \{\text{both heads}\}$ with $P(A) = \tfrac14$, and $Y$ indicates $B = \{\text{at least one head}\}$ with $P(B) = \tfrac34$. Both heads certainly means at least one head, so $A \subseteq B$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = \tfrac14 \cdot \tfrac14 = \tfrac1{16} = 0.0625$. The covariance is positive, as expected: learning that both tosses were heads guarantees that at least one was.
solution.shortcut: When one indicator implies the other ($X = 1 \Rightarrow Y = 1$), $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = P(X = 1)\,P(Y = 0)$. Here that is $P(\text{HH}) \cdot P(\text{TT}) = \tfrac14 \cdot \tfrac14 = \tfrac1{16}$.
solution.commonTrap: Taking $E[XY] = E[X]\,E[Y] = \tfrac3{16}$ as if $X$ and $Y$ were independent, which makes the covariance $0$. Both variables are defined from the same two tosses and are strongly dependent: $XY = X$, so $E[XY] = \tfrac14$. A second slip is misreading $Y$ as "exactly one head" ($P = \tfrac12$) instead of "at least one head" ($P = \tfrac34$). Then $XY = 0$ on every outcome and the covariance becomes $0 - \tfrac14 \cdot \tfrac12 = -0.125$, with even the sign wrong.

answerVerification.checkCode:
from fractions import Fraction as F
from itertools import product
out=list(product('HT',repeat=2)); p=F(1,len(out))
X=lambda o: 1 if o==('H','H') else 0
Y=lambda o: 1 if 'H' in o else 0
EX=sum(p*X(o) for o in out); EY=sum(p*Y(o) for o in out); EXY=sum(p*X(o)*Y(o) for o in out)
cov=EXY-EX*EY
print('E[X]=',EX,'E[Y]=',EY,'E[XY]=',EXY,'Cov=',cov,'=',float(cov))
print('rounded to 3 dp:', round(float(cov)+1e-12,3), '| truncated:', int(float(cov)*1000)/1000)
